cnv-council-valente-tony.text:
Everyone needs to be able to choose how they move around. Whether you walk, roll, drive or take transit, you should be able to do so safely and responsibly. And it should be fun too!

The City has built new protected mobility corridors, including Esplanade, Crosscut Bridge, and West 1st Street. These projects improve connections with our neighbours and help create a more complete transportation network. This work is not just about bikes. It is about freedom, independence, and accessibility, especially for people with disabilities, seniors, and anyone who uses mobility supports and needs safe, connected routes to move through the city.

There is more to do, and we need to continue working closely with the District of North Vancouver, TransLink, and our regional partners — but we are making real progress. Together with TransLink, we helped bring RapidBus service to the North Shore, supported by dedicated bus lanes that now move thousands of commuters more efficiently every day. The next step is Bus Rapid Transit: a faster, more reliable form of bus service with dedicated lanes, priority at intersections, frequent service, and better stations to move more people without requiring everyone to drive.

Experience here and around the world shows that we cannot simply build our way out of traffic congestion. The only real way to manage traffic is to give people better options. When more people can choose transit, walking, rolling, cycling, or other forms of mobility, our streets work better for everyone — including those who drive. These alternatives to single-occupancy vehicles are not just cheaper, cleaner, and more efficient; they also help make our city healthier, more accessible, and more fun.

Move public transit forward – Bus Rapid Transit creates bus priority to ensure people using transit are rewarded with time and advocate for a new Second Narrows crossing that enables public transit

Vote to create a safe and complete mobility network for all ages that supports transportation choices

Support active living by expanding shared transportation options and supporting improved lighting and sidewalks for pedestrians

By creating more housing options we can ensure more accessible and affordable housing options for all.

The City has made real progress in diversifying the shapes and sizes of homes available in our community. We have focused new housing near major corridors and frequent transit, including areas now supported by RapidBus service. This helps give more people the option to live close to work, school, services, and transportation.

Today, many new rental projects are coming online. Over the last eight years, the City has seen its largest increase in rental homes since the 1970s. I have supported stronger protections for long-time renters and worked to ensure people impacted by redevelopment receive support to relocate and remain connected to their community.

Looking ahead, I will continue to support more purpose-built rental housing, non-market housing, co-operative housing, co-housing, and workforce housing. We need homes for people across incomes — including seniors, youth, families, essential workers, and those most at risk of being pushed out.

We also need to better integrate rental housing with local commercial areas, including retail and office developments. The most vibrant and livable cities in the world combine homes, shops, services, public spaces, and transit so people can meet more of their daily needs close to home.

Housing is about more than buildings. It is about whether people can build a life here, stay connected to their community, and see a future for themselves in the City of North Vancouver.

Create more housing options in the right places by focusing new homes near frequent transit, services, shops, schools, and public spaces — while ensuring development contributes fairly to community amenities.

Support more affordable and non-market housing by expanding co-op, social, co-housing, workforce, and non-market options through federal and provincial funding, partnerships, and municipal tools.

Protect people through change by strengthening renter protections, supporting residents through redevelopment, and prioritizing long-time residents, seniors, youth, workers, and vulnerable households

Managing and expanding municipal assets that ensure our quality of life is essential. The majority of our population lives in multi-family buildings without lots of outdoor spaces, so supporting public spaces is critical to enjoying our city and enhancing community connections.

When people live in apartments, condos, co-ops, and townhomes, shared public spaces become even more important. Parks, plazas, playgrounds, dog parks, street trees, sidewalks, mobility routes, sports courts, community facilities, and welcoming streets all become part of people’s everyday living space.

That is why I will continue to support investments in infrastructure and public spaces that serve the vast majority of our residents. Great public spaces help make compact living more livable, support mental and physical health, create opportunities for fitness and social connection, and strengthen the North Shore lifestyle we all value.

Public spaces also support local businesses and our local economy. When people have great places to gather, walk, shop, eat, play, and spend time, our commercial areas become more vibrant and resilient.

I have supported initiatives to expand public amenities across the city, including new parklets, more dog parks, expanded street tree coverage, improved active transportation connections, and new skate park facilities.

A more affordable city must also be a more livable city. That means building homes, but also investing in the public spaces and infrastructure that allow people to thrive.

Create greener, better-connected neighbourhoods by protecting mature trees, expanding street tree coverage, securing more green space through development, and supporting green mid-block pedestrian connectors, pocket parks, and improved access to transit.

Invest in accessible, people-focused public spaces with washrooms, seating, shade, trees, play areas, dog spaces, parklets, outdoor art, and gathering places that work for people of all ages and abilities.

Protect quality of life as the city grows by managing urban noise, addressing impacts from landscaping equipment, modified vehicle exhausts, and construction, while securing access to important recreation amenities like tennis and pickleball courts.

Expand small-scale public spaces across the city through parklets, barklets, dog runs, pocket parks, outdoor art, and better pedestrian connections that make dense neighbourhoods feel more livable, social, and green.

Championing small businesses, local entrepreneurs, and nationally significant employers, so our city remains vibrant, diverse, and prosperous.

A strong local economy means a stronger North Vancouver. When more people can work, shop, access services, and run businesses close to home, we reduce pressure on our transportation network and give people back more time with family, friends, and community.

Our economy is diverse and more significant than many people realize. Alongside our growing health-care sector, North Vancouver is home to major employers and nationally significant companies connected to the port, trade, marine, industrial, and export sectors. These businesses provide good local jobs, support regional supply chains, and play an important role in Canada’s economy — especially at a time when the country is under pressure to strengthen productivity, trade, infrastructure, and economic resilience.

Many small and family-run businesses are under real pressure. They are struggling to find workers, manage rising costs, and absorb high property taxes. This is where housing affordability, transportation, public space, and economic sustainability all come together. If people who work in North Vancouver cannot afford to live here — or cannot get here efficiently — local businesses, services, and institutions all feel the impact. That is why we need to advance workforce housing, improve transportation options, and continue investing in vibrant streets, plazas, patios, parklets, markets, events, and welcoming commercial areas that bring people together and support the foot traffic small businesses depend on.

The City’s updated 2024 Economic Strategy gives us a stronger framework to support this work, with a focus on strengthening employment lands, making it easier to do business, creating world-class public places, and building a resilient local economy. It also identifies opportunities to grow the health and innovation cluster around Lions Gate Hospital and revitalize Central Lonsdale as a destination for community and commercial activity. The creation of the Central Lonsdale Business Improvement Area is an important step, giving local businesses and property owners a stronger collective voice to support events, beautification, marketing, safety, and economic vitality in one of the City’s most important commercial districts.

Advocate for fairer business taxation so small businesses are not unfairly burdened by property taxes based on the “highest and best use” of land.

Build on our economic strengths by supporting health and innovation around Lions Gate Hospital, film and creative industries in Bridgman, and the port, marine, trade, and export sectors.

Advance workforce housing so more people who work in North Vancouver can afford to live here.

Support vibrant commercial districts through business improvement associations, better public spaces, patios, parklets, events, and welcoming streets.

Improve goods movement by exploring logistics hubs and practical solutions that reduce congestion while supporting local businesses.
cnv-council-valente-tony.title: Policy - Tony Valente

cnv-council-valente-tony.text:
Tony Valente brings eight years of experience on City Council and a unique combination of skills, experience, and passion to his role as a Councillor in the City of North Vancouver. He is a seasoned infrastructure project and risk management leader, an urban thinker, and a dedicated community volunteer.

A graduate of both St. Thomas Aquinas Regional Secondary School and the UBC Sauder School of Business, Tony holds a Bachelor of Commerce and an MBA. Early in his career, he spent three years in Milan, Italy, working in logistics and product management for Whirlpool Europe.

After returning to British Columbia, Tony completed his MBA at UBC Sauder, specializing in strategic management and accounting.

For nearly 20 years, Tony has worked on major infrastructure projects and in risk management, taking on increasingly senior leadership roles. He now works full-time as Senior Director, Infrastructure and Capital Projects for a BC Crown corporation.

Since 2010, Tony has also given his time to his community — first by serving on his strata council, and subsequently in a series of advisory and committee roles with the District and City of North Vancouver.

A proponent of public spaces for people to enjoy their city and streets — making our community a place to gather and celebrate in the outdoors — Tony was a founding member and Director of the North Van Urban Forum, a non-profit organization addressing urban issues and encouraging consultation and transparency on the North Shore.

The group organized Project Waterfront: North Van Design Jam to stimulate discussion and engagement with citizens on the future development of Lot 5 – now the Shipyards on the lower Lonsdale waterfront. Tony was also part of the branding committee resulting in Lot 5 becoming “The Shipyards.”

Tony’s other passion is transportation. As a former Chair for the HUB Cycling North Shore Committee, as well as in a variety of other local volunteer roles, he has worked with the community on cycling infrastructure and safety improvements for all ages and abilities, as well as e-bikes, ride-sharing, and a variety of other active transportation issues.

Tony and his wife, Elena (and cat Oliver Spritz) live in Lower Lonsdale, and when not devoting most of their time to work and volunteering, they enjoy travelling to look for ideas for how to make our city even better.

“Linda is an ally and a tireless advocate for the entire 2SLGBTQ+ community. She has taken every opportunity to advance inclusion, equity, and love. “Everyone in our community should feel welcome and included. As an immigrant and as a person with a disability I understand this better than most people. “Working with Mayor Linda Buchanan on strengthening the bond between the City and the School District has been a joy. I admire her commitment to public service, providing inclusive spaces for everyone, and working collaboratively together. I am deeply grateful that she puts the needs and wellbeing of children at the forefront of her work. Linda has become a true friend. I couldn’t be happier that she is seeking re-election.”

“Linda Buchanan is a trailblazing Mayor. She is committed to truly understanding the lived experience of residents in order to deliver on priorities for the City Of North Vancouver. “Only Linda can lead the City of North Vancouver forward. Over her two terms as Mayor, she has proven that through unwavering optimism, collaboration, and hard work that a better community is possible. She has always listened and put people first.”

cnv-mayor-buchanan-linda.text:
Linda was first elected Mayor of the City of North Vancouver in November, 2018. Her goal is to build a healthy and inclusive city where people come first.

As Mayor, she has established herself as a leader both on the North Shore and throughout Metro Vancouver. She is proud to serve as Chair of Metro Vancouver’s Invest Vancouver Management Board as well as a member of the TransLink Mayors’ Council on Regional Transportation where she is Chair of the Public Affairs and Governance Standing Committee. As a member of the TransLink Mayors’ Council and Chair of North Shore Connects, she has led the charge to secure rapid transit to the North Shore.

Prior to her election as Mayor, Linda served as a member of North Vancouver City Council from 2011 to 2018 and prior to that she was an elected Trustee on the North Vancouver School Board.

Born and raised in the City, Linda has deep roots in North Vancouver. Her father, Jim Buchanan, was a popular teacher and principal whose name is given to the annual “Buchanan Bowl” football match between Carson Graham and Handsworth high schools and the James Buchanan Theatre at Argyle secondary school. Her mother, Verna, has served the community in a volunteer capacity for decades. Linda credits her parents for her love for the community and public service.

Linda holds a Bachelor’s Degree with Honours in nursing from the University of British Columbia. Prior to her election as Mayor, Linda worked for close to 30 years as a public health nurse for Vancouver Coastal Health delivering preventative nursing services and immunization programs to the general public, members of the Squamish Nation, and in North Shore schools and community clinics. In 2019, she received the UBC School of Nursing Centenary Medal of Distinction for her achievements in nursing and in 2023 she received the UBC Faculty of Applied Science Dean’s Medal of Distinction for excellence in her field.

Linda’s first involvement in civic politics came through her role in helping to secure funding for the heritage preservation and renovation of Ridgeway Elementary School, one of the City’s most important heritage properties. She is a founding member of the Ridgeway Heritage Society.

Linda lives in the Ridgeway/Grand Boulevard neighbourhood with her husband, Kevin, where they raised their four children. They enjoy riding their bikes along the Spirit Trail, listening to jazz music, and supporting the local arts and culture scene.

cnv-mayor-buchanan-linda.text:
Access to affordable and adequate housing is a right we all share. But we know not everyone in our community is well housed, and we know there is more work to do. That’s why I’m committed to continue partnering with stakeholders, senior levels of government, and others to deliver housing that meets the needs of families, youth, and seniors who call our city home – or hope to.

Delivered hundreds of new housing – affordable, supportive housing, rental housing, and market housing. Including Senior’s Safe House and SAFER units

Delivered 89 below-market rental homes through the completion of Phase 1 of the North Shore Neighbourhood House Hub Development

Delivered a new family respite centre – financed and operated by CareBC providing support to seniors and families

Advanced North Shore Neighbourhood House Phase 2 Hub Development, including a mass timber building with 179 rental homes, 30% below-market, and a new North Shore Neighbourhood House – these phases represent the single largest investment in non-market housing in a generation on public lands

Secured $18.6 M in federal funding to support and modernize housing policies to speed up delivery, expand affordability and invest in infrastructure

Updated the Mid-Market Rental Policy to improve eligibility criteria, a fair and transparent tenant selection process

Advanced the Development Application Process Review to improve the development approvals process from end to end

Adopted the new Housing Needs Report – planning for current and future housing needs

Championed new home financing opportunities for first-time buyers such as rent-to-own homes

Strengthened the City’s Residential Tenant Displacement Policy

Advanced work on supporting residents during extreme heat events in multifamily buildings

Convened North Shore Homelessness Action Initiative, an assembly of North Shore officials with a mutual commitment to enhance the coordination and action to prevent and alleviate homelessness in our communities
cnv-mayor-buchanan-linda.title: Housing – Linda Buchanan

cnv-mayor-buchanan-linda.text:
Moving efficiently and safely through the community is a priority we all share. Increasingly, people are asking for transportation alternatives that are more affordable and healthier. For too long, cities have been designed with the car in mind, and this hasn’t provided people with the transportation options they need today and as their lives change. That’s why I’m focused on advancing a range of mobility improvements that will make it easier for everyone to get around — regardless of how you choose to travel.

Secured the accelerated extension of the R2 Rapid Bus delivering a stronger connection between the North Shore and Metrotown which began in September

Secured increased Seabus and HandyDart service, and a new rapid bus connection between Lynn Valley and Lonsdale

Delivered Crosscut Bridge across Highway 1 improving the safety of people who actively move through the City

Delivered infrastructure to improve Safe Routes to School including new signalization, painted crosswalks, and traffic calming

Delivered new protected mobility lanes improving safety for all road users and expanded our sidewalk network, including new curb letdowns to improve accessibility, walking and active movement for all ages while supporting access to transit, commercial areas and other key destinations such as schools, the hospital and its surrounding campus

Delivered the Esplanade Complete Street Project improving safety and public realm

Approved the Safe Mobility Strategy, the New Mobility Strategy (updated transportation plan) and Walk CNV Strategy

Implemented the first ever Electric Bike Share Program in BC with record-level ridership in North America which now includes e-cargo bikes

Partnered with the Province of BC on a Micro-Mobility pilot program and implemented an educational program on the safe use of Electric Bikes

Delivered a new Marine Drive Mosquito Creek Bridge with dedicated mobility lanes

Continue to move forward on the Upper Levels Greenway and Lonsdale Highway Overpass improvements

Implemented a new Curb Access and Parking Plan to better manage parking, support businesses and improve access in high-demand areas

Adopted the Electric Vehicle Strategy and delivered several new fast charging stations

HUB Cycling 2026 Biggest Leap Award for leadership in active transportation
cnv-mayor-buchanan-linda.title: Transportation – Linda Buchanan

cnv-mayor-buchanan-linda.text:
Public safety is fundamental to a healthy, connected city. It is about more than responding when something goes wrong — it is about prevention, preparedness, trust, and the everyday confidence people feel in their neighbourhoods, public spaces, workplaces, and homes. Over the past several years, we have strengthened emergency preparedness, improved coordination across agencies and invested in the tools that help us better understand and respond to community concerns. As our city grows and the risks around us become more complex, from extreme weather to social challenges to emergency events, we must continue building a community where people feel safe, supported, and prepared.

Improved Public Safety Coordination through internal working groups and the Creation of the Community Safety Advisory Committee

Advanced Emergency preparedness through disaster resilience assessments, evacuation planning, Emergency Operations Centre training and active threat preparedness

Advanced Extreme heat and climate risk planning in partnership with neighbouring municipalities and Nations

Installed Noise monitoring stations and have used to support enforcement, planning and community well-being

Improved emergency response time by upgrading10 intersections with fire pre-emption technology, with 15 additional intersections planned for 2026

Dave Kurvers · Candidate for Mayor · City of North Vancouver

Better City services. Housing that fits people’s lives. Practical action to make it easier to get around.

The campaign now has a complete seven-part platform. Each area begins with a clear commitment and keeps the supporting detail available for people who want to look deeper.

Local government should make everyday life easier to navigate—and be candid about how well it is performing.

Tell people what to expect from City Hall, measure performance and publish the results.

Plan housing, transportation, parks and services around how people actually live.

Clear service standards, productive administration, responsible budgets and public accountability for major projects.

Business retention, faster approvals, measurable local-business health and commercial streets that work.

Homes with enough space, useful layouts, secure tenure and options for different stages of life.

Transportation ideas that fit North Vancouver, reliable access and better local and regional connections.

Meaningful choices before major planning decisions, protected public land and infrastructure alongside growth.

More useful shared space, disciplined recreation projects and public places designed for everyday community life.

The right response from the right service, accessibility from the beginning and practical relationships that deliver results.

Applicants should know the requirements, who is responsible for the file and when they can reasonably expect an answer. These standards cover the City’s portion of the process and do not waive provincial or other legal requirements.

For an application that is complete, compliant and within the City’s portion of the process.

Where the use is permitted and all City requirements have been satisfied.

Clear requirements, published service standards, productive administration, resilient budgets and public accountability for major projects.

These standards apply when an application is complete and compliant. They cover the City’s portion of the process and do not waive provincial health, liquor, fire, building, safety or other legal requirements.

Straightforward applications that are complete and compliant.

Where the use is permitted and all City requirements are satisfied.

Publish a complete checklist before an applicant spends money.

Run internal reviews in parallel where possible rather than serially.

Publish the percentage of files meeting the service standard.

Identify repeat-review causes and fix the workflow rather than normalizing rework.

If we don’t measure how City Hall performs, we can’t manage it or improve it.

Use machines for repetitive work. Use people for judgment and public service.

Automation and AI can help with permit completeness checks, routine zoning and document pre-checks, missing-material detection, workflow routing, status communication and searches of internal technical information.

Benchmark Development Services using turnaround time, files completed per staff member, cost per application, repeat review cycles, customer feedback and the percentage of applications meeting service standards.

Review whether permit fees can fall as the cost per file falls

Important distinction: permit and application fees support administration. Growth-related infrastructure charges should not become a substitute for an inefficient permitting bureaucracy.

Can City Hall balance the books if development slows for three years?

Before approving each five-year financial plan, publish a normal case, a slow-growth case and a severe-slowdown case.

Materially lower permit activity, development revenue and tax-base growth for three years.

A prolonged downturn without assuming reserves can cover the gap indefinitely.

Temporary growth revenue should not create permanent spending problems.

Major City projects should have one public record that preserves the complete cost, schedule, scope and financing history.

Also required for significant municipal debt or the sale or long-term lease of strategic City land.

Triggered by a cost increase above 20 percent, a delay beyond six months, or a material change in scope or financing.

If the cost, schedule, scope or financing changes materially, show the public what changed before simply moving on.

Keep annual tax increases close to inflation where practical.

Show the real dollar effect on representative households and businesses.

Separate ongoing revenue from one-time or growth-related revenue.

Show which operating costs are growing faster than inflation and why.

Direct unexpected development or assessment growth first toward reserves, infrastructure, debt reduction or tax stabilization before creating permanent commitments.

The goal is simple: a City government we can afford in good years and slower ones.

Strengthen disclosure expectations for elected officials and senior staff, particularly around development, procurement and significant land transactions.

Stronger public reporting around development, procurement and significant land transactions

A culture where conflicts are declared before controversy arises

New investment is welcome, but the City should first make sure businesses already here can survive, expand and reinvest.

A complete, straightforward business-licence application should receive a City decision within one week. Commercial tenant improvements should also have published service standards.

Carry forward lawful approvals and infrastructure when a new business takes over substantially the same use, wherever legally possible.

A City that says it is open for business should be able to show how long it takes to open one.

City delay has a cost, even when it never appears in the City budget.

A business can burn rent, wages and working capital while waiting for approvals. City reporting should show where delay occurs and how often applicants must repeat work.

Measure the tradeoffs before and after changing a commercial street.

Before major changes to parking, loading, vehicle access, curb allocation, streetscape design or prolonged construction, publish a short business-impact assessment. After implementation, measure what actually happened.

Before City Hall changes access to a commercial street, it should know what businesses depend on that access and measure what happens afterward.

Publish a clear picture of whether local businesses are thriving or being displaced.

The City should publish a full Local Business Health Report annually, supported by quarterly service and permitting measures.

Encourage small, adaptable commercial units and narrow storefronts where appropriate.

Use stable and transparent terms in City-owned commercial premises.

Explore relocation or return opportunities for established businesses displaced by redevelopment.

Evaluate lawful provincial tax-relief tools where appropriate.

Advocate for better commercial-lease disclosure and transparency.

The City cannot impose residential-style rent controls on private commercial leases.

Spread more of the Shipyards’ energy through Lonsdale and selected commercial areas without defining vibrancy as alcohol-oriented nightlife.

Evening cafes, restaurants, dessert shops and independent retail

Practical location and noise rules that protect nearby residents

Give visitors reasons to explore Lower and Central Lonsdale and other commercial areas.

Support resident-hosted visitor accommodation where it does not remove ordinary long-term rental housing.

Help residents remain connected to their community as their needs change.

Whether one regional line serves dispersed North Shore trips

Protect station and access opportunities in land-use planning.

Avoid waterfront decisions that foreclose future rail access.

Plan the Quay as one multimodal node rather than disconnected terminals.

Service details and timing would depend on corridor engineering and a viable business case.

Measure occupancy, turnover, accessibility, customer experience and business effects.

Your first interaction with a neighbourhood should not be a parking app.

Keep the existing short free period straightforward and visible.

Consider merchant validation and pay-on-exit in appropriate City lots.

Measure user difficulty and abandoned transactions, not only occupancy.

People should not be penalized for the vehicle their job requires.

Plan off-street hubs where shared vehicles can park, charge, clean and wait.

Provide managed pickup and drop-off space at major destinations.

Design new parking structures so they can be converted if demand changes.

Do not assume a specific deployment date for autonomous fleets.

A good sidewalk moves people. A great sidewalk also gives people a reason to stay.

cnv-mayor-mcgraw-mike.text:
Regular Meet the Mayor events, open and unscripted. My door is open, and I won't be hard to find.

Real debate and public input before decisions are made, not after. Only 22.4% of us voted last time; that's a signal.

The North Shore covers 37% of the wastewater plant's cost on 8% of the region's population. That's not fair.

Real growth, on the terms residents were promised, with the public voice back in the room.

Real feedback from residents, business owners, and community voices across North Vancouver.

I’ve known Mike McGraw for over 20 years, since our kids played football together at Handsworth. Since then, I’ve watched him thrive as a successful entrepreneur, have a wonderful family life with … lots of fun vacations and successful adult children, and serve with dedication as an elected school trustee. Trust is the foundation of leadership, and Mike shows it through savvy financial decision-making, true collaboration and patient listening. He loves North Vancouver and will be a great Mayor.

I’ve been involved in North Vancouver community issues for more than 30 years — protecting parks, advocating for meaningful public input and working to make our city a better place to live. Over the … past several months, I’ve had many conversations with Mike McGraw about the challenges facing our city. What has impressed me most is that Mike listens. He asks questions, considers different viewpoints and understands that City Hall belongs to the people who live here. The next four years will bring major decisions about growth, parks, renters, traffic, infrastructure and how we spend public money. I strongly believe Mike can help bring City Hall back to the community — with residents heard, taxpayers respected and North Vancouver’s future carefully planned. That is why I am proud to endorse Mike McGraw for Mayor.

I met Mike over 10 years ago when we were volunteering on a North Van community board. Mike is one of the most emotionally intelligent leaders I’ve met. When he says his plan is to show up, listen … and lead; I have no doubt that is exactly what he will do. He will be an outstanding Mayor for the CNV!

Mike demonstrates strong leadership through his integrity, responsiveness, and proactive approach to problem-solving. He has a remarkable ability to delegate responsibilities appropriately while … maintaining accountability through diligent follow-up, resulting in effective governance and positive outcomes for our community.

I’ve had the pleasure of witnessing Mike in action as President of our condo’s Strata Council, and I’ve been consistently impressed by his leadership. He is exceptionally responsive, organized, and … task-oriented. When an issue comes up, he takes it seriously, follows through in a timely manner, and works diligently to find practical and fair solutions. Just as importantly, he believes in being transparent and keeping people informed. I know I can trust Mike to listen, consider different perspectives, and make thoughtful decisions with the best interests of our community in mind. He is a driven leader who truly cares about our building and the people who live here. His commitment, accessibility, fairness, and ability to get things done have made a real difference, and I’m extremely appreciative of the time, effort, and dedication Mike has put into our building and the people who call it home. Knowing Mike and seeing how he leads, I can only imagine the positive impact he could have in a larger role serving North Vancouver.

Mike has been the chair of the Strata Council where I own a condo. He would do an excellent job as Mayor of North Vancouver. As a member of the board I have seen over a few years how hard Mike works … and how committed he is to getting things successfully accomplished. Mike is respectful of others and understands governance processes very well. I have felt extremely fortunate that Mike was chair of our board and I have great confidence he would bring those same skills to the role of Mayor.

I’ve known Mike McGraw for about 20 years, first as a customer at my business, then socially. Over the years I’ve seen how measured, smart, and thoughtful he is, and how well he listens. He served on … the CNV school board, and now that he’s retired from his business, he’s back and focused on fixing this city’s issues, economic and otherwise. You can count on him to bring some real common sense to City governance, which has been sorely lacking for a long time. I like Mike very much. He’s a stickler for detail, process, and rules, and one of the most trustworthy people I’ve ever met. He says what he means and means what he says, which is refreshing in a world of bafflegab politics. I highly and unreservedly endorse Mike McGraw for Mayor of The City of North Vancouver.

As president of the largest residential strata in the City, I vetted Mike firsthand. He listens, respects residents, and will honour the social contract of the OCP. He brings business acumen, fiscal … discipline, and an open-door policy. Proud to stand as an official nominator for our next Mayor.

I spent 30 years as a corporate consultant specializing in organizational development. … I was skilled at assessing talent. Mike McGraw is a highly skilled leader. At this pivotal time in the City of … North Vancouver, we require a Mayor who will work with Council focused on meeting or exceeding the needs of the 68,000 plus residents before all others. I’ve had the chance to work with Mike closely and can personally attest to his strong value-based approach to problem solving. He is warm and funny, he listens and learns, he gives a damn, and it shows. His tool kit includes many years of being a servant leader, a manager committed to the well being of his staff. Mike learned that running a business required he become a prudent and fiscally responsible manager of the company’s resources, which is exactly what the City needs right now. And he will bring fairness and balance back to decision making. … Not many people would sell their business and retire, then volunteer to run for public office, Mike did. … Electing Mike McGraw as Mayor along with new, fresh voices on Council will transform how the City of North Vancouver operates and delivers services to all of us who call CNV home.

Mike McGraw’s run for mayor is the much needed breath of fresh air the City of North Vancouver’s residents have been hoping for in 2 long decades. It’s about time we had a mayor whose interests are … rooted in the public good, and I can’t wait to help him get elected on October 17th.

Having Mike as our strata president has given me a front-row seat to what genuine community leadership looks like. He’s remarkably proactive, always stepping up to handle building priorities head-on … , and consistently takes residents’ needs into account before major decisions are made. Mike has also managed our budget with real fiscal discipline, keeping our strata fees stable and predictable without sacrificing quality or upkeep. He’s fair, transparent, and as approachable as they come. Mike brings people together to solve practical problems, and those exact qualities will make him an outstanding Mayor for the City of North Vancouver

I’ve worked with Mike McGraw on our strata council for over two years. As president, he has been accessible to residents, fair with suppliers and effective in addressing issues. Most importantly, he … has fostered a collaborative environment on the strata council where everyone plays to their strengths to get things done.

As our Strata President, Mike is always approachable, great communicator, attention to detail, gets the job done and keeps costs in check.

I love this city. North Vancouver has been my home for decades, and I built a software company here that created more than 20 highly skilled, well-paying local jobs. After a long career in business, I’m stepping away from it to serve this community again. A lot of people have told me their voice doesn’t matter at City Hall, and I think they have a point. I want a council that debates the hard questions instead of rubber-stamping them, with real public input before decisions are made, not after. Rebuilding that starts with showing up and listening, so here’s my promise: Show up. Listen. Lead.

“A lot of people have told me their voice doesn’t matter at City Hall. I think they have a point.”

Whether it's five dollars, five minutes, or a free Saturday, there's a way to pitch in that fits.
cnv-mayor-mcgraw-mike.title: McGraw for Mayor | City of North Vancouver

cnv-mayor-mcgraw-mike.text:
My door is open. Rebuilding trust starts with showing up and listening. That's why I'll hold regular Meet the Mayor events: open, unscripted, where residents can ask hard questions and get straight answers. You shouldn't need an appointment or a connection to talk to your mayor. Residents won't wait a year to hear from me directly: I'll deliver a free, public State of the City address within my first six to eight months.

That number isn't apathy. It's a lot of people who've concluded their voice doesn't matter at City Hall, and I think they have a point. Too often, "public engagement" means being brought in only after the plan is already decided - a survey to check a box, not a real chance to change anything. Not every decision needs a public vote, but residents deserve real debate while a decision can still move, not a rubber stamp once it can't.

We're being forced to shoulder more than our fair share of the cost overruns at the wastewater plant, under a regional cost-sharing formula that loads a heavier tax burden onto North Shore residents than the rest of the region. Costs keep climbing, and even after two rounds of letters and votes demanding independent oversight, the cost-sharing formula still hasn't changed.

It's not just the wastewater plant. Five years ago, City Hall had essentially no debt; today it's authorized roughly $165 million in borrowing for Harry Jerome and the North Shore Neighbourhood House alone, on top of our share of a wastewater plant where the North Shore covers 37% of the cost despite being 8% of the region's population. Worthwhile projects can still come with real financial risk, and residents deserve a mayor who's straight with them about what's already committed, and what still needs to be worked out, before signing off on the next one.

The province requires some density near transit, and that's fair. What wasn't required: a density transfer that pushed a 21-storey tower onto an East 14th Street block the OCP itself capped at 6 to 8, or restricting residents to written comments only, a step beyond what the province's own rules require. It's one example among several of decisions getting made without residents at the table. As Capilano Mall, the ICBC lands, and Lonsdale Great Street move forward, that's the standard I'll hold to.

Growth done right should also mean growth the city can actually move around. I want real capacity for walking, cycling, and transit alongside the roads we still rely on, built in from the start, not bolted on after the gridlock arrives. This is the city I love: mountains, ocean, and trails minutes from downtown, a place worth getting right as it grows.

Today’s decisions should work for every generation and make it possible for the next one to build a life and stay in North Vancouver.

You don't have to wait until I'm elected. Ask me something now.

We raised our three children here. I built a software company here that created more than 20 highly skilled, well-paying local jobs. After a long career in business, I'm stepping away from the private sector to return to public service - because this community has given me a lot, and I'm not done giving back.

Known to generations as the Outdoor School, now home to an Environmental Learning Centre.

That's the job I do today as a volunteer: budgets, maintenance, legal risk, and the different needs of 57 homes and 10 businesses under one roof. It's unglamorous, and it's exactly the kind of work City Hall is supposed to be good at.

Have we talked at your door, a coffee meet-up, or a community event?

This is where those stories will go. If I've knocked on your door or you've met me somewhere around the city, tell me about it. With your permission, I'd love to share it here.

dnv-council-anderson-daniel.text:
The North Shore is in trouble. Our public facilities are aging, roads and sewers are wearing out, and costs keep climbing. Development has become unaffordable and is outpacing the infrastructure needed to support it. We need strong, pragmatic voices who will keep budgets on track and ensure essential services are delivered efficiently. I believe the District of North Vancouver works best when decisions are made locally. My mission is to restore control over community planning, hold regional bodies accountable, and invest in infrastructure that supports responsible growth. I will protect our environment, respect taxpayers, and fight to make housing attainable for young families—preserving the balance that makes the North Shore a place where people, nature, and community thrive together.

If we want a municipal system that is rooted in common sense, reflective of the community it serves, and focused on liveability, we need to put in the work at a local level. Join me in that mission!
dnv-council-anderson-daniel.title: Daniel Anderson for District Council

dnv-council-anderson-daniel.text:
Since provincial bills have stripped local governments of planning power, Victoria’s one-size-fits-all density model is failing the North Shore—our unique terrain, infrastructure limits, and neighborhood character can’t be ignored. Rigid density quotas and clawed-back zoning powers leave councils unable to balance housing with infrastructure, green space, and livability. That’s not planning; it’s planning from a distance.

If elected, I will petition Victoria to repeal Bill 44 and restore municipal authority over community planning, while strengthening community oversight of District finances through purpose-built committees.

The $600 “poo palace” levy is an albatross around every North Vancouver resident’s neck for the next 30 years. Metro Vancouver’s bloated structure and runaway costs burden taxpayers and drain resources that should strengthen our communities. When a regional body can impose massive commitments without accountability, the system is broken.

If elected, I will fight for real Metro Vancouver reform from day one—demanding transparency, fiscal responsibility, and a fair deal for residents. And I’ll lead by example: every dollar I earn from Metro Vancouver will be donated back to the District I serve.

What makes North Vancouver special is balance, a community where people can enjoy both nature and city life, in a way few places can offer. Our population is just the right size to sustain vibrant neighborhoods while still protecting the parks, forests, and public spaces that define us. But that balance is at risk. Infrastructure must keep pace with growth and be supported by adequate services and local business policies. To ease transportation pressure and ensure emergency services reach our communities quickly, we must advocate for reliable, convenient, and affordable transit and petition the province for new options along our overburdened central corridors and bridges.

The dream of starting a family in the same community you grew up in is slipping away, and that should concern all of us. When young people are priced out, we don’t just lose residents; we lose the next generation of our community’s identity. A thriving city needs continuity, not constant turnover. To change course, we have to make sure new development is liveable, affordable, and built to last. That means local governments must play their part,reviewing the cumulative costs they impose on new builds, supporting projects that meet long-term housing needs, and pushing for fairer policies at the provincial and federal level. Right now, white-collar management teams are earning twice what skilled builders make on the same projects. If we don’t tackle those imbalances and reduce development costs, we’ll never make housing attainable again. Density must be targeted in the right regions through thoughtful zoning, balancing housing needs with livability and long-term sustainability. A restructured municipal government can maximize efficiencies and unlock innovative revenue streams to ease budget pressures. It’s time to build homes that regular families can actually live in, not just invest in.

Across North America, too many of us are “bowling alone.” We are disconnected from our neighbours and community life. Yet research shows that strong civic engagement is the heartbeat of effective, responsive government.

I believe local government can help rebuild those connections by creating accessible community spaces, offering fair rental rates, and supporting events that bring people together. For the past ten years, I’ve organized weekly gatherings that build trust and belonging. I know firsthand how powerful that sense of community can be. My goal is to jumpstart civic participation and turn our neighbourhoods into thriving, connected communities once again.
dnv-council-anderson-daniel.title: Why I'm Running — Daniel Anderson for District Council

dnv-council-anderson-daniel.text:
Daniel Anderson (H.BA, M.A., M.T.) is a school teacher and resident of the District of North Vancouver. First elected as a School Trustee in 2022, Dan has spent the past four years helping to govern one of the province’s most respected school districts.

In office, Dan has focused on strengthening core learning — tackling declines in literacy and numeracy — while ensuring responsible financial management. As chair of the Audit Committee, he led the rebuilding of the district’s strategic reserves and championed greater transparency in spending. He also introduced a successful motion to enshrine non-partisanship in the B.C. School Trustees Association’s foundational documents, underscoring his belief that education should always prioritize students over politics. Dan has been a vocal advocate for age-appropriate learning and limited screen use in classrooms. Dan is equally committed to accountability beyond education. As spokesperson for the North Shore Neighborhoods Alliance (NSNA) — a coalition of seven community associations — he has worked to expose the soaring costs of the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant and has called for both provincial relief and an independent public inquiry under Section 764 and Section 765 of the Local Government Act.

Dan moved to the North Shore in 1998. He played soccer throughout high school and graduated from Sutherland Secondary in 2009. Dan has a labrador retriever named Nietzsche who he loves to take on walks around his new home, in Lynn Creek. Dan has been the associate director of the Vancouver Institute of Philosophy for Children since 2014. During his time with the organization, he has focused on publishing papers aimed to improve classroom thinking. Dan has received over eight awards for his contributions to academia and Canadian education, including a 2018 SSHRC Canadian Graduate Scholarship, and the 2021 Wilfred Rusk Wees Fellowship.

Dan is turning his attention to municipal politics because he believes our community is at a crossroads. The systems that support us all are under strain, housing is slipping further out of reach for young people, and too many local decisions are being shaped by Metro Vancouver and distant powers in Victoria. For the past four years, Dan has fought for his community: now he’s ready to bring that fight, and his experience, to council.

dnv-council-bond-mathew.text:
The next Council will make tough decisions to balance affordability and quality of life. District residents are paying hundreds of millions of dollars for the over-runs at Metro Vancouver's Wastewater Treatment Plant. We cannot allow failures on that scale to happen again. We must invest responsibly in infrastructure, transportation, public facilities and services to maintain and improve the quality of life we've all come to enjoy.

Major capital projects need careful oversight and clear accountability. Council must understand costs and risks, test assumptions, demand clear reporting and explain the consequences to residents.

Infrastructure, transportation, public facilities and services shape daily life in North Vancouver. The District must maintain what people rely on, plan ahead and invest with a clear understanding of long-term value and cost.

Affordability and quality of life belong in the same conversation. People at every stage of life should be able to build roots, stay connected and see a future in North Vancouver.

Every candidate cares deeply about our community. Council is strongest when its members each bring their unique experience to the table and test decisions from more than one perspective.

I bring two terms on District Council, a record of community volunteering and nonprofit leadership, and more than 15 years as a professional engineer working on major transportation infrastructure. I also know from my own life what it means to choose North Vancouver, work to find a suitable home, raise children here and manage the everyday cost of living in this community. Together, these experiences help me bring people together, work through complex problems and keep Council decisions grounded in how they affect daily life.

Our neighbours, friends and families can build roots, stay connected and thrive in North Vancouver at every stage of life. That vision guided me when I was elected to Council in 2014, a few months before my eldest daughter was born. She is now eleven and her sister is nine. Building a healthier, happier and more resilient community has never mattered more to me.

I am running again to help Council make responsible decisions, protect what people value about North Vancouver, and keep building a community where we can all make a good life.

dnv-council-bond-mathew.text:
North Vancouver is where I am raising my two daughters, where I have built deep community connections and where I want to keep contributing to the future of our community.

My approach to public service was shaped long before I entered politics. My parents moved from Ontario to the Lower Mainland and built a home-renovation business during the difficult economy of the early 1980s, a business they still run today. As a child, I travelled with my mom as she picked up cheques, paid bills and signed contracts, and I spent time working with my dad on job sites around Metro Vancouver. Their hard work, dedication and determination shaped my character and taught me what it takes to build something that lasts.

I graduated from Simon Fraser University in 2008 with a Bachelor of Applied Science in Systems Engineering and a Certificate in Sustainable Community Development. I carried a full-time engineering course load, maintained the grades needed for a scholarship and worked part time to pay my way through university without a student loan.

My career has included work in both the private and public sectors. For the first ten years of my engineering career, I travelled across British Columbia, working on complex transportation problems and implementing practical solutions. In 2018, I stepped away from full-time engineering to focus on caring for my young children. During that time, I balanced parenting with consulting engineering, bicycle courier work, community volunteering and service as treasurer of the Lynn Valley Parent Participation Preschool. In 2022, I returned to full-time engineering work. My career now spans more than 15 years and includes major transportation infrastructure projects.

Throughout my career, I have kept learning through formal training and by looking at how other communities tackle transportation, land use, housing, sustainability and climate change. That work has taught me to connect the different parts of a problem, test assumptions, identify risks early and follow decisions through to implementation. It has also reinforced my duty as an engineer to put public safety, health, welfare and the natural environment first.

I believe in service and giving back to the community. From 2008 to 2013, I served as president of the North Shore Mountain Bike Association. During that time, a volunteer group with more work than time or money grew into an organization with paid staff, strong partnerships with businesses and local governments, and an engaged membership. My role was to help set a clear direction, build the team and nurture the relationships needed to get things done. I am proud that successive boards and staff have continued to grow the organization.

In 2014, District residents elected me to Council, and I served two terms through 2022. My roles included serving as alternate to the TransLink Mayors’ Council, Council liaison to the Major Infrastructure Projects Advisory Committee and Heritage Advisory Committee, and a member of the Finance and Audit Committee and Metro Vancouver Housing Committee. I advocated for affordable housing partnerships, safer active transportation and open, accountable public decision-making. That experience taught me what local government can accomplish, where it depends on partnerships, and how much good decisions rely on listening, preparation and clear priorities.

I do not pretend to have every answer. I try to listen carefully, ask practical questions and clearly explain the trade-offs in the decisions before us. I am running again because the District faces major decisions about infrastructure, transportation and long-term costs. I want to bring my experience, passion and grounded way of working back to the Council table.

Most campaigns lead with promises. I want to lead with a standard, because the promises only mean something if you know how I'll actually behave once the cameras are off and the hard votes come up.

Good governance isn't complicated. Show up. Have a plan. Be honest. Do what you said you'd do. That's the job. It's easy to say and harder to live up to, which is exactly why it's worth putting in writing before you've given me your vote rather than after.

This page is about the kind of councillor I intend to be. It is not a list of promises. Promises are specific, they can be checked, and they belong on the Commitments page where you can hold me to them.

What follows is the part that comes before that. How I will show up, how I will decide, and what I will tell you when I get something wrong.

Residents deserve leadership that listens and is present, not just in the weeks before an election. Too many decisions get made without most people ever hearing about them until the outcome is already set.

I'll be at the table, in the community, and reachable in between. That includes making a real effort to reach the people councils usually talk past: renters, younger families, and residents like me who will live longest with the choices this council makes. If a decision is going to shape the District for thirty years, the people who'll be here in thirty years deserve a say in it.

Good intentions don't fix aging infrastructure, and they don't bring down the cost of living here. The work is in the details, and the details take homework.

I come to the table prepared. I read the budgets, I dug into the files, and I will bring forward ideas that hold up to scrutiny rather than ones that just sound good in a headline. I'd rather show up with a workable idea and get told no than show up with nothing. And I'll be honest about what one councillor among seven can and can't deliver, because a plan that oversells itself isn't a plan, it's a pitch.

Trust starts with clear communication and open budgets, even when the news is hard. You can't trust a council that only tells you the easy half of the story.

That means plain language instead of process jargon, real numbers instead of reassurance, and a straight answer when the answer is difficult. When I don't know something, I'll say so. When I get something wrong, I'll own it. The goal isn't to look right, it's to give residents an accurate picture of where things actually stand so you can hold your council to it.

Accountability isn't a slogan. It only counts if you can check it.

So I'll publish my voting record and keep it public, so you can measure my choices against the commitments I made to earn your vote. If I said I'd push for something and then voted the other way, you should be able to see that plainly and ask me why. That's the one promise I can keep entirely on my own, without needing four other votes to get there, and I intend to keep it.

A note on transparency. This page has evolved as the campaign has grown. If you'd like to see where it started, the earlier version of my core values is still public here . Nothing disappears, nothing gets quietly edited.

Each priority below lists what changes. These are campaign positions — where a number is quoted, its source is named at the foot of the page.

Within 100 days of taking office, I will publish a personal commitment tracker and seek Council support for an official municipal delivery dashboard.

The tracker will show original deadlines, Council decisions, outside dependencies, progress and evidence of completion. Proposed budgets and Council-approved budgets will be shown separately.

Updates will be published every quarter. Delays, revised targets and commitments that do not proceed will be explained openly.

Within six months of taking office, I will bring forward an initial implementation plan covering every priority and neighbourhood commitment. It will show existing District work that already meets part of each one, the extra staff time and spending needed, first-year actions versus later-term projects, and which items depend on funding or Council decisions.

The estimated program cost has grown from about $700 million to $3.86 billion. I believe North Shore ratepayers should not carry that increase alone.

Settlement money: Metro Vancouver received a $235 million settlement from the original contractor in May 2026. I will press for the largest possible share of those funds to benefit North Shore ratepayers, and for a public accounting of how the settlement is allocated.

Independent inquiry: I will support a full, independent inquiry into the cost overruns, and push for the fullest lawful public release of Metro Vancouver’s review and government responses.

Fair cost-sharing: I will seek Council’s appointment as the District’s representative on the Metro Vancouver board, and advocate for fairer regional cost-sharing. I will ask Victoria and Ottawa for capital funding, debt-servicing help and targeted ratepayer relief.

Resident petition: I will launch a North Shore wastewater fairness petition, open to residents, businesses and neighbouring councils.

Quarterly reports: I will report every quarter on advocacy, government responses and funding decisions, including what any relief means for a typical household bill.

Every dollar justified before Council asks residents for more.

In my first year, I will propose a core service review to find savings, duplication and services that could be delivered better.

I will seek Council support to set an annual budget target that holds the increase in the municipal property-tax levy on existing properties at or below inflation, measured by the previous year’s B.C. all-items Consumer Price Index. Any proposed increase above that benchmark will come with a public explanation of its causes, alternatives and effect on services. Utility fees, and costs set by Metro Vancouver, the Province or TransLink, will be shown separately.

Each budget will include a plain-language breakdown: what the District controls, what it does not, and what a typical homeowner and business will pay.

New spending in this platform will be funded from savings or partner contributions wherever possible. Grants will not be counted until approved, and any tax impact will be stated before Council votes.

A first-term target of securing sites, approvals and funding partnerships for 1,000 affordable rental and co-op homes.

I will work with non-profit, co-operative and other qualified housing partners on suitable District-owned and partner lands. The focus is rental and co-op housing, where affordability can be protected long-term.

What “secured” means: progress will be tracked at each stage: site identified, site secured, project approved, financing committed, under construction and occupied. A home will count toward the 1,000 target only once its site is secured, the project is approved and its financing is committed.

Affordability will be defined before any project is approved: income bands by household size, maximum rents (and whether utilities are included), and how long the affordability terms last, with a goal of at least 60 years.

Within my first year, I will bring forward a feasibility and financing plan naming available sites, realistic capacity, affordability levels and milestones. It will pursue provincial programs through BC Housing, including BC Builds for middle-income homes, and federal programs. Because BC Builds does not provide the ongoing subsidies lower-income households need, the plan will show separately how deeper affordability would be funded. No funding will be counted until committed.

If the evidence requires changes to the target, I will explain them publicly.

Where the law and funding agreements allow, I will support transparent local-connection criteria for residents facing displacement and people who work in our community, considered alongside income and housing need.

Read the full plan: who decides, what Max proposes, the trade-offs

A public list of District bottlenecks within 100 days, better coordination to reduce avoidable overlapping closures, and simpler resident parking at parks.

Within my first 100 days, I will seek Council support to publish an initial ranking of ten priority District traffic bottlenecks, using available delay, safety and traffic data, and flag where more study is needed before work can be designed.

I will bring forward a phased improvement plan with estimated costs, funding options and early actions.

I will propose a shared construction calendar that coordinates municipal, utility and development roadwork. Emergency work and projects controlled by others will be clearly marked.

On Highway 1, the bridges and the Ironworkers approach, which the Province controls, I will press the Province and TransLink for timelines and for coordination with District roadwork.

Park parking: I will propose simpler annual registration for the resident parking pass at parks including Deep Cove, Panorama and Whey-ah-Wichen / Cates, an option for people without smartphones, and fewer unnecessary repeat check-ins. A lot-by-lot review will balance turnover, accessible spaces and longer stays. Some changes may depend on the operator contract and technology, and any change will state its cost and effect on availability.

No major rezoning or District growth plan without a clear public answer on District infrastructure, who pays, and what depends on schools and transit.

I am not anti-housing. I am pro-infrastructure: new homes need the water, sewer, roads, schools and transit to support them.

I will propose public infrastructure-capacity and financing statements for major discretionary rezonings and District-led growth plans, consistent with provincial law. “Major” will be defined by Council using clear thresholds, such as the number of homes or floor area.

Each statement will show existing District capacity for water, sewer, drainage and roads, required upgrades, expected timing and who is expected to pay. It will separate confirmed funding from proposed contributions.

Schools, transit and other services controlled by partner agencies will be reported separately, as dependencies the District cannot guarantee.

The process will build on existing engineering work, with independent review where a project’s scale or risk warrants it.

One coordinating contact at Municipal Hall for your business, and a pilot for livelier evenings in our town centres.

I will propose a business concierge: one coordinating contact for commercial applications, expansions and small-business renovations.

I will ask for current processing times to be reported publicly, then propose realistic service targets based on that data, including a coordinated first response and a target time to decision for defined categories of complete applications. Reports will separate District review time from time waiting on applicants or outside agencies, and the proposal will include a staffing and cost assessment.

Processing times, missed targets and fixes will be reported publicly every quarter.

I will seek Council approval for a one-year evening activity pilot with businesses and community groups: food vendors, small live performances, community talent nights and voluntary extended hours. It will have a set budget, accessibility and operating conditions, and will be judged on attendance, neighbourhood impacts, safety and business results.

Investment outreach will focus on film, digital production and clean technology, while supporting the businesses already here.

Faster municipal reviews and an assessment of District spaces for childcare.

I will propose a priority review stream for new and expanding childcare facilities, with early coordination between applicants, District staff and Vancouver Coastal Health.

I will seek an assessment of underused District-owned spaces that could host childcare, including conversion costs, accessibility and operating viability. Where feasible, operators will be chosen through a transparent process. Provincial capital funding will be pursued, but no space or grant will be counted until it is confirmed.

Success will be measured by licensed spaces that actually open. Provincial licensing and safety rules remain in full effect.

Students deserve safe schools, safe routes home and protection from drug trafficking and exploitation.

I will seek a coordinated school-safety plan with North Vancouver RCMP, the North Vancouver School District and community partners to assess reported drug activity near schools and identify where more prevention and enforcement resources are needed.

I will advocate for visible patrols and focused enforcement where police evidence identifies trafficking or threats to students, while respecting the RCMP’s responsibility for operational decisions.

I will support clear reporting channels for students, parents and school staff, alongside drug education, early intervention and access to youth support services.

The District’s draft 2026–2030 financial plan shows RCMP staffing at 119 members, unchanged from 2025 and down from 129 in 2022, and anticipates a return to historical levels by 2030. I will request a public explanation of both the reduction and the restoration schedule, including whether it can be accelerated, separating authorized positions, funded positions, vacancies and officers available for duty.

Where the assessment identifies staffing gaps affecting public safety, I will bring forward a costed proposal with Council and the RCMP.

I will seek regular public progress reports that protect students’ privacy and ongoing investigations.

A risk-ranked plan with real targets, and a plan for residents who can’t simply drive away.

Working with North Shore Emergency Management, and seeking collaboration with neighbouring First Nations, I will support alert tests, tabletop exercises and voluntary community drills.

Plans will address people without vehicles, residents who need assistance and accessible emergency communication.

Preparedness will cover wildfire, smoke, extreme heat, flooding, earthquakes and power outages. Public guidance will make clear that real-time emergency instructions always come first.

What this campaign does with your information, what this website is, and how to tell us when something on it does not work for you.

Only what you type into a form on this site. That may include your name, email address, telephone number, postal code, neighbourhood, address (for lawn sign requests), languages spoken, availability, the issues you care about and your message.

The site does not ask for, and must never be used to collect, financial account details, government identification numbers or passwords.

To meet record-keeping obligations under BC election law, where those apply.

Your information is used by the campaign team only. It is not sold, rented or traded . It is shared outside the campaign only where the law requires it — most relevantly, Elections BC requires campaigns to report contributions of $100 or more, including the contributor's name.

Campaign records are kept for as long as BC election law requires and are then deleted. If you ask to be removed from campaign communications before then, that request is honoured immediately.

Unsubscribe — every campaign email carries a working unsubscribe link, and you can also email the campaign directly.

Access — ask what the campaign holds about you and it will be provided.

Correction and deletion — ask for a correction or removal and it will be actioned, except where election law requires a record to be kept.

This site sets no advertising or tracking cookies, and carries no third-party analytics, advertising pixels or social media trackers. Opening a page contacts no company other than the one hosting it — the typefaces are served from this domain rather than from Google Fonts — with one exception: the map of voting places on the voting page, which is served by Google and loads as you scroll down to it. The Instagram posts at the top of the homepage are not an exception: this site’s own server fetches them from Instagram and serves their pictures itself, so your browser contacts Instagram only if you tap a post or the “Follow on Instagram” link. Your browser may store small preferences locally — a chosen language, whether you picked the light or dark theme, or an unsent form draft — which stays on your device and is never sent to the campaign. The only cookie this site ever sets is for the campaign’s own administrator while logged in; visitors get none.

The campaign counts visits to its own pages, on its own server, to see which pages people read and roughly where interest is coming from. Each page view sends one small message to this website containing the page, the site that linked to it (if any), your browser’s language setting, the width of your screen (to tell a phone from a desktop) and, on the voting page, which language you chose. No cookie is set and no outside service is involved. Your network address is used for two things and then discarded: to look up an approximate location — usually a city — in a database held on the campaign’s own server, and to make a scrambled daily identifier that lets the campaign count how many different people visited on a given day. That identifier changes every day and cannot be turned back into an address, so nobody can be followed from one day to the next, and the address itself is never stored. If your browser sends a Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control signal, nothing is sent at all. Counts are kept for no more than 13 months.

The campaign’s videos, the short one on the homepage, the eight-minute one and the short ones on the Farsi, Chinese and Tagalog pages, are served from this website, not from YouTube or any other company. If you play one, the same kind of message records that it was played, on which page, how many seconds of it you watched, the furthest point you reached and whether it reached the end, with the same scrambled daily identifier and the width of your screen. To keep those as one record, the page makes up a random code for that single page view; the code is not stored on your device and is gone when you leave the page. Nothing is recorded if you do not press play, or if your browser sends a Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control signal.

The voting page shows the District of North Vancouver’s map of voting places, which is served by Google Maps. It is not requested when the page opens; your browser loads it as you scroll down to the “Where to vote” section — at which point Google receives the request and may set its own cookies, as it would on any site carrying a Google map. The District’s own website, linked beneath the map, carries the same map.

The voting page, and the Chinese, Farsi and Tagalog pages, can show the voting places nearest you. It works on your own device: the page downloads one list of North Vancouver postal codes and their approximate positions from this website, and your browser compares your postal code with it. Your postal code is not sent to the campaign or to anyone else, and nothing is kept. If you press “Use my location”, your browser asks your permission first and then tells the page where you are; that stays on your device too, although your browser may use its own location service to work it out. The “Directions” links open Google Maps, which then receives the address of the voting place you chose, and nothing else from this site.

If you sign up for voting reminders or campaign updates, your name, email address, mobile number (if you gave one) and area are stored in a database on the campaign’s own server, outside the public web folder. No email-marketing company holds the list. The campaign records the date and time you agreed, the address the form was sent from, and the exact sentence you ticked, because Canada’s anti-spam law asks for that record. Emails are sent from this domain; every one carries a working unsubscribe link and the headers that let your mail program unsubscribe you in one click. Text messages are sent only to people who ticked the separate text-message box, through Twilio, a messaging carrier that receives your number and the message and nothing else; reply STOP to any text to end them. Unsubscribing closes that channel immediately. The record itself is kept for as long as BC election law requires and is then deleted.

The poll questions are anonymous. An answer is stored on the campaign’s own server with the question, the option chosen, the area you gave if you gave one, and the same scrambled daily identifier the visit counter uses, so that one person counts once per question per day. No name, email or address is stored with an answer, and nothing joins an answer to the contact list. Your browser remembers which questions you have answered so it can show you the results; “Change my answer” forgets that and your next answer replaces the earlier one for the day. Results for a question are shown to anyone who has answered it, with the number of answers, and the two questions marked “for the campaign only” are never shown to anyone outside the campaign.

If your connection drops while you are filling in a form, your answers are kept in your own browser so they are not lost. They stay on your device until you send them or clear your browser data.
