Thirty-eight years in North Vancouver. A business owner, an operations manager and a neighbour who believes a municipal government should be able to explain itself.

Max Zahedi is an independent candidate for Mayor of the District of North Vancouver, British Columbia, in the municipal election on Saturday, October 17, 2026. He has lived in North Vancouver for 38 years. He holds an MBA in Global Management and a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science. He has owned and operated businesses, managed operations, worked in government and regulatory settings, written policy and procedures for a Crown corporation, and served on three strata councils. He speaks English and Farsi. His campaign focuses on accountability for the cost of the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant, property taxes, housing, traffic, public safety and a more responsive municipal hall. He is not part of any party or slate.

On the ballot as Fardin Maximilian Zahedi . Max is the name he goes by.

This is where I built my life, raised my family and became part of a community I deeply care about. Through my work in technology, public service, business and community organizations, I have learned the value of listening, working with others and following through.

I am running for mayor because I know this community, understand the pressures residents are facing and believe I have the experience to improve how the District works for them.

I have watched a necessary public project — the North Shore Wastewater Treatment Plant — grow from a reported $700 million estimate in 2013 to $3.86 billion in 2024, and I have watched residents struggle to get a straight answer about how that happened or what it means for their tax bill. That is not a failure of engineering. It is a failure of reporting, oversight and accountability, and those are things a mayor can actually change.

In my working life, a project that tripled its budget would have triggered a review, a written explanation and a change in how the next one was run. Residents deserve the same standard from the government closest to them.

But this campaign is not only about one plant. It is about property taxes people can plan around, housing that matches what the infrastructure can carry, streets that are not permanently under construction, a district prepared for wildfire and earthquake, and a municipal hall that answers the phone.

My education is in both business and technology — an MBA in Global Management and a Bachelor of Science in Computer Science. That combination shapes how I approach public problems: understand the system, measure what it actually does, and report the result honestly even when it is not flattering.

Professionally I have worked in software engineering, owned and run businesses, managed operations, worked within government and regulatory environments, and consulted for other business owners. I have also spent years in community and cultural leadership across the North Shore.

My family lives here. My business life has been here. The trails, the creeks and the neighbourhood shops are not talking points to me — they are where I have spent the last four decades.

Publish the numbers, including the ones that are inconvenient.

Treat residents as the people who pay for this, because they are.

dnv-trustee-khan-raheela.text:
Thank you for being here. Every career has a "why." Mine began in the financial markets, working at the intersection of economics, investment strategy, and public influence. From managing institutional portfolios to collaborating with regulators, shaping PR and media strategies, and sharing financial insights on television. I spent years in fast-paced, high-impact work shifting systems at an economic level.

Over time, I recognized a recurring barrier: self-exclusion. I saw how cultural confidence and self-doubt often caused people to opt out of pathways before they even began.

Today, my work centers on youth, communities, and systems. I focus on building cultural confidence and life skills, creating pathways that ensure everyone has the tools to participate fully. ​

My story is one of transition from finance to purpose, from metrics to meaning. It’s about building bridges across cultures, generations, and systems, and using knowledge, access, and experience to open doors for others. ​ For a long time, my world revolved around numbers, managing financial portfolios, markets, performance. I built a successful career in global finance, managing large-scale investments across regions and economies. On paper, it all made sense. Yet, somewhere along the way, I began to notice what the numbers didn’t show: the people left out of the system, the untapped potential, and the quiet cost of exclusion.

Working across both emerging economies and established western systems gave me a front-row seat to how access (or the lack of it) shapes lives. I saw how financial systems could either empower communities or unintentionally widen social gaps.

My education at Oxford and Yale, and my experience as a Yale World Fellow, sharpened my global perspective but it was lived experience that truly shifted my path. Becoming a mother changed the way I understood leadership, resilience, and responsibility. It made equity personal. It made inclusion urgent.

I experienced, firsthand, how easy it is for people especially women, immigrants, and newcomers to shrink themselves, to self-exclude, or to feel they don’t quite belong. That experience became the catalyst for my community work. I began creating and leading programs focused on cultural confidence, integration, and financial literacy first for adults, then for children. I wanted to start early, to give children the tools I wish more of us had growing up: confidence in who they are, comfort with money, and a sense of agency in the world. Teaching financial literacy from the preschool years onward became one of the most meaningful parts of my work.

Another outcome of this transition took shape while living in Canada, a country with open borders and a welcoming, multicultural environment that aligns closely with my equity initiatives. This inspired me to develop a children’s book designed to help young readers build cultural confidence. I am also working on a second book project focused on financial literacy, introducing basic concepts of money in a developmentally appropriate way and helping children develop essential life skills and healthy financial habits that support long-term success.

​Leaving a successful financial career wasn’t a loss; it was a deliberate choice. I transitioned into leadership development and equity-focused work because I believe real growth happens when systems are designed with people at the center. Today, my work focuses on advancing diversity, equity, and inclusion, empowering women and youth, and supporting responsible funding that creates both impact and sustainability.
